newsitem.title: PERU: Peaceful end to Peru hostage crisis seems possible.
newsitem.headline: Peaceful end to Peru hostage crisis seems possible.

text.p: A peaceful end to Peru's 12-day-old hostage crisis looked more possible on Sunday after the government and Marxist rebels still holding 83 VIP captives softened "no compromise" positions and met face-to-face for the first time.

President Alberto Fujimori sent his mediator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, for a long meeting on Saturday with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini inside the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.
The fruit of that meeting was immediate: the release of 20 hostages, leaving 83 behind.

With the exception of several 1993 meetings Fujimori had with Abimael Guzman, the jailed leader of the Shining Path guerrilla movement, no government official has held direct talks with Peruvian insurgents in 16 years of conflict.
In a statement read by one of the newly-freed captives, the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas expressed a willingness "to withdraw from the occupied residence by way of dialogue."
The communique, which struck a more conciliatory tone than the rebels' two previous statements, made no mention of their main condition -- the release of around 400 jailed comrades.
The rebels had initially threatened to kill their hostages if their colleagues were not freed. As of Sunday they had released more than 420 of the original captives.

Backing up the new mood, the MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, told Reuters on Sunday the rebels were prepared to negotiate their original demand and could settle for an "intermediate solution."

"We still insist on the liberation of the political prisoners, but we consider that an intermediate solution can be reached," he said in an interview from Hamburg. Asked what that meant, he said: "Not necessarily the liberation of all the political prisoners."
He declined to give any further details of the rebel negotiating position and did not say what other components a political solution to the stand-off might entail.
But he said the release of the 20 hostages on Saturday by the rebels was a gesture of flexibility in response to the government's first face-to-face meeting with the MRTA.

Palermo said following the release of the 20 hostages -- mostly Peruvian diplomats and Japanese businessmen -- that there had been "advances for the solution of this serious incident", but gave no details.
Palermo stopped short of giving the full imprimatur of the state to his talk with Cerpa, saying their conversation was "oficioso" -- a Spanish term which can mean unofficial or semi-official.
But the meeting was still a virtually unheard-of gesture from the Fujimori administration.
The moves brought fresh hope in Peru, where the population is weary of guerrilla violence and embarrassed by the international attention caused by the current crisis.
"The danger of a violent way out is growing more distant," the anti-government daily La Republica said on its front page.

"The most important news in these 12 days of captivity has been that the MRTA did not, in yesterday's communique, ask for the freedom of its prisoners but rather, in all cases, for the improvement of the jails' situation," wrote columnist Jaime De Althaus in the daily Expreso. "It is an gigantic step forward, which raises the prospect of a way out."
In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Rutaro Hashimoto welcomed the new signs but warned against over-optimism.

"It is not time yet to get our hopes up but reading the guerrillas' demands, it seems possible to have a dialogue with the rebels," he told reporters. He said the remaining hostages were still facing a "tough situation".

In a letter to Hashimoto carried out by nine Japanese hostages released on Saturday, the still captive Japanese, numbering about 20 diplomats and businessmen, warned their situation was becoming more dangerous.

"If the situation in which heavily-armed soldiers keep a close watch on us lasts for a long time, it will become extremely difficult for us to keep the balance between mind and body," the letter said.
Hashimoto said he planned to contact Fujimori, himself the son of Japanese immigrants to Peru, to see if negotiations could be speeded up.
Early on Sunday, the area around the ambassador's residence was quiet. Heavily armed police continued to cordon off an area of two city blocks on each side of the building.
Besides the Japanese, Fujimori's brother, Pedro, and a handful of high-ranking Peruvian police and government officials were still being held in the residence.

A police source told Reuters three experts from the United States were in Lima helping Peruvian police analyse conversations inside the residence, which were being picked up by surveillance teams using electronic eavesdropping devices.
The source, who declined to be named, also said other U.S. experts were advising Peruvian troops preparing for a possible last-resort assault on the compound.
